name: Nendran banana chips & Nendran banana cultivation
tagline: Kerala’s crunchy classic — from fresh Nendran harvests to coconut‑oil chips
summary: Nendran is Kerala’s signature cooking banana: harvests fill local markets in season and small producers turn firm Nendran fingers into thin, coconut‑oil fried chips (upperi).
description: Nendran is the cooking/plantain type that Kerala uses for chips, sweets and many home recipes. The variety is prized for firm, starchy fingers that hold shape when fried.

Banana chips (upperi) are a small craft industry across Malabar and Palakkad: thin slices of raw Nendran deep‑fried and salted, traditionally in coconut oil, then packed by family makers and small shops.
For visitors this means lively market stalls and small 'chips kadas' where you can watch or buy freshly fried chips, and seasonally stacked green bunches at wholesale markets and roadside sellers.

Nendran cultivation runs on an annual cycle (about 10–12 months) and farmers time plantings for festival demand; harvests and market flows shift by planting date and weather, so local supply varies year to year.
highlights: Nendran — Kerala’s classic cooking banana used for chips and festive cooking
Upperi (banana chips) — thin, crisp slices fried traditionally in coconut oil
Small farms and family‑run chips makers supply Kozhikode and Palakkad markets
Seasonal price and supply swings — demand spikes around Onam and festivals
Farm cycle ~11 months; ratoon crops give a second harvest without full replanting

sections.heading: Background
body: Nendran is the main commercial plantain variety in Kerala and forms the backbone of the state’s chips and many cooked banana dishes. It occupies a large share of local banana plantings and is cultivated both rainfed and with irrigation.

Farmers plant suckers and bring bunches to harvest roughly 10–12 months later; producers grade hands for chips or fresh markets. Kerala research and extension bodies publish cultivation packages to improve yields and soil health.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Visit city and town markets in Kozhikode and Palakkad to see green Nendran bunches stacked for sale; small chips shops (chips kadas) fry fresh batches during the morning and late afternoon.

Watch the traditional technique: thin slicing, deep frying until golden, quick salting while hot — many makers still use coconut oil for the characteristic aroma and crunch. Buy small packets to taste different house blends and textures.
If you can, ask the seller where the fruit comes from — local farms, neighbouring districts or Tamil Nadu supply show in the pile‑ups at wholesale yards.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Nendran supply runs through much of the year but peaks and quality depend on planting cycles and the monsoon. Expect market activity and festival demand from late summer into winter; confirm local availability before travelling for a specific purchase.

Buy in small quantities if you want fresh chips: packed chips keep longer, but chips eaten within a few days taste best. When sampling or buying fresh fruit for cooking, check for firm fingers and a clean cut on the stalk.

latest.text: Nendran prices hit a multi‑year peak ahead of Onam, with farmgate rates reported above ₹70/kg as supply falls in some High Range areas.
Market reports note that local supply in late July 2026 was thin and many Palakkad arrivals came from Satyamangalam (Tamil Nadu), pushing lower‑grade fruit to snack makers.

visitorInfo.bestTime: September–April is the main harvest window; festival demand peaks around Onam (Aug–Sep).
visitorInfo.howToReach: Kozhikode and Palakkad are on major road and rail routes; reach local markets by town bus, auto or taxi and ask for central produce/wholesale markets or well‑known chips shops in town centres.
etiquette: Ask vendors whether chips are fried in coconut oil if you want the traditional flavour.
Buy a small pack first — fresh upperi are best within a few days; packed, sealed packets store longer.
If buying fresh Nendran for cooking, look for firm, unbruised fingers and a clean stalk cut. Confirm origin if you need local Kerala fruit vs arrivals from neighbouring states.
Festival periods (Onam) raise prices and demand — confirm availability before planning purchases.
